segments.text: [[p0]] is a terminal multiplexer: it enables a number of terminals to be created, accessed, and controlled from a single screen. [[p1]] may be detached from a screen and continue running in the background, then later reattached.

When [[p0]] is started, it creates a new [[p1]] with a single [[p2]] and displays it on screen. A status line at the bottom of the screen shows information on the current session and is used to enter interactive commands.

A session is a single collection of [[p0]]pseudo terminals[[p1]] under the management of [[p2]]. Each session has one or more windows linked to it. A window occupies the entire screen and may be split into rectangular panes, each of which is a separate pseudo terminal (the [[p3]] manual page documents the technical details of pseudo terminals). Any number of [[p4]] instances may connect to the same session, and any number of windows may be present in the same session. Once all sessions are killed, [[p5]] exits.
Each session is persistent and will survive accidental disconnection (such as [[p0]] connection timeout) or intentional detaching (with the ‘[[p1]]’ key strokes). [[p2]] may be reattached using:

[[p0]] stores the server socket in a directory under [[p1]] or /tmp if it is unset. The default socket is named [[p2]]. This option allows a different socket name to be specified, allowing several independent [[p3]] servers to be run. Comments are marked by the unquoted # character - any remaining text after a comment is ignored until the end of the line.

If the last character of a line is \, the line is joined with the following line (the \ and the newline are completely removed). This is called line continuation and applies both inside and outside quoted strings and in comments, but not inside braces.

Command arguments may be specified as strings surrounded by single (') quotes or double quotes ("), or as command lists surrounded by braces ({}). This is required when the argument contains any special character. Single and double quoted strings cannot span multiple lines except with line continuation. Braces can span multiple lines.

Environment variables preceded by $ are replaced with their value from the global environment (see the [[p0]] section).
A leading ~ or ~user is expanded to the home directory of the current or specified user.

When preceded (escaped) by a \, the following characters are replaced: \e by the escape character; \r by a carriage return; \n by a newline; and \t by a tab.
\ooo is replaced by a character of the octal value ooo. Three octal digits are required, for example \001. The largest valid character is \377.

Any other characters preceded by \ are replaced by themselves (that is, the \ is removed) and are not treated as having any special meaning - so for example \; will not mark a command sequence and \$ will not expand an environment variable.

The [[p0]] server manages clients, sessions, windows and panes. Clients are attached to sessions to interact with them, either when they are created with the [[p1]] command, or later with the [[p2]] command. Each session has one or more windows [[p3]] into it. Windows may be linked to multiple sessions and are made up of one or more panes, each of which contains a pseudo terminal. Commands for creating, linking and otherwise manipulating windows are covered in the [[p4]] section.
The following commands are available to manage clients and sessions:

If run from outside [[p0]], attach to [[p1]] in the current terminal. [[p2]] must already exist - to create a new session, see the [[p3]] command (with [[p4]] to create or attach). If used from inside, switch the currently attached session to [[p5]]. If [[p6]] is specified, any other clients attached to the session are detached. If [[p7]] is given, send [[p8]] to the parent process of the client as well as detaching the client, typically causing it to exit. [[p9]] sets a comma-separated list of client flags. The flags are:
the client does not affect the size of other clients

The search commands come in several varieties: ‘[[p0]]’ and ‘[[p1]]’ search for a regular expression; the ‘[[p2]]’ variants search for a plain text string rather than a regular expression; ‘[[p3]]’ perform an incremental search and expect to be used with the [[p4]] flag to the [[p5]] command. The default incremental search key bindings, ‘[[p0]]’ and ‘[[p1]]’, are designed to emulate [[p2]]. When first pressed they allow a new search term to be entered; if pressed with an empty search term they repeat the previously used search term.

The ‘[[p0]]’ and ‘[[p1]]’ move between shell prompts, but require the shell to emit an escape sequence (\033]133;A\033\\) to tell [[p2]] where the prompts are located; if the shell does not do this, these commands will do nothing. The [[p3]] flag jumps to the beginning of the command output instead of the shell prompt. Finding the beginning of command output requires the shell to emit an escape sequence (\033]133;C\033\\) to tell tmux where the output begins. If the shell does not send these escape sequences, these commands do nothing.

Copy commands may take an optional buffer prefix argument which is used to generate the buffer name (the default is ‘[[p0]]’ so buffers are named ‘[[p1]]’, ‘[[p2]]’ and so on). Pipe commands take a command argument which is the command to which the selected text is piped. ‘[[p3]]’ variants also copy the selection. The ‘[[p4]]’ variants of some commands exit copy mode after they have completed (for copy commands) or when the cursor reaches the bottom (for scrolling commands). ‘[[p5]]’ variants do not clear the selection. All the copy commands can take the [[p6]] and [[p7]] flags. The [[p8]] flag suppresses setting the terminal clipboard when copying, while the [[p9]] flag suppresses adding a paste buffer with the text.

The next and previous word keys skip over whitespace and treat consecutive runs of either word separators or other letters as words. Word separators can be customized with the [[p0]] session option. The three next and previous space keys work similarly but treat all non-whitespace characters as part of a word. Setting [[p1]] to the empty string makes next/previous word equivalent to next/previous space.

The jump commands enable quick movement within a line. For instance, typing ‘[[p0]]’ followed by ‘[[p1]]’ will move the cursor to the next ‘[[p2]]’ character on the current line. A ‘[[p3]]’ will then jump to the next occurrence.

[[p0]] offers various options to specify the colour and attributes of aspects of the interface, for example [[p1]] for the status line. In addition, embedded styles may be specified in format options, such as [[p2]], by enclosing them in ‘[[p3]]’ and ‘[[p4]]’.
A style may be the single term ‘[[p0]]’ to specify the default style (which may come from an option, for example [[p1]] in the status line) or a space or comma separated list of the following:

Set the foreground colour. The colour is one of: [[p0]], [[p1]], [[p2]], [[p3]], [[p4]], [[p5]], [[p6]], [[p7]]; if supported the bright variants [[p8]], [[p9]], ...; [[p10]] to [[p11]] from the 256-colour set; [[p12]] for the default colour; [[p13]] for the terminal default colour; or a hexadecimal RGB string such as ‘[[p14]]’.
Set no attributes (turn off any active attributes).
Set an attribute. Any of the attributes may be prefixed with ‘[[p0]]’ to unset. [[p1]] is the terminal alternate character set.
Align text to the left, centre or right of the available space if appropriate.
Fill the available space with a background colour if appropriate.
Dim foreground and background colours by [[p0]].
Set the width of the styled area. [[p0]] may be a column count or a percentage (for example ‘[[p1]]’).

Make the styled text an OSC 8 hyperlink to [[p0]], for example ‘[[p1]]’. This is emitted only to terminals with the [[p2]] feature (see [[p3]]); it works in the status line and in other formats drawn with styles. The link continues until [[p4]], [[p5]], or an empty [[p6]] is given. The [[p7]] may not contain spaces or commas and is limited in length.

Mark the position of the various window list components in the [[p0]] option: [[p1]] marks the start of the list; [[p2]] is the part of the list that should be kept in focus if the entire list won't fit in the available space (typically the current window); [[p3]] and [[p4]] mark the text to be used to mark that text has been trimmed from the left or right of the list if there is not enough space.

Do not copy attributes from the default style.

Mark a range for mouse events in the [[p0]] option. When a mouse event occurs in the [[p1]] or [[p2]] range, the ‘[[p3]]’ and ‘[[p4]]’ key bindings are triggered.

These trigger the ‘[[p3]]’ mouse key with the target session, window or pane given by the ‘[[p4]]’ argument. ‘[[p5]]’ is a session ID, window index in the current session or a pane ID. Set the current colours and attributes as the default, overwriting any previous default. The previous default cannot be restored.

[[p0]] distinguishes between names and titles. Windows and sessions have names, which may be used to specify them in targets and are displayed in the status line and various lists: the name is the [[p1]] identifier for a window or session. Only panes have titles. A pane's title is typically set by the program running inside the pane using an escape sequence (like it would set the [[p2]] window title in [[p3]]). Windows themselves do not have titles - a window's title is the title of its active pane. [[p4]] itself may set the title of the terminal in which the client is running, see the [[p5]] option.
A session's name is set with the [[p0]] and [[p1]] commands. A window's name is set with one of:
A command argument (such as [[p0]] for [[p1]] or [[p2]]).
An escape sequence (if the [[p0]] option is turned on):
Automatic renaming, which sets the name to the active command in the window's active pane. See the [[p0]] option.
When a pane is first created, its title is the hostname. A pane's title can be set via the title setting escape sequence, for example:
It can also be modified with the [[p0]] [[p1]] command.

When the server is started, [[p0]] copies the environment into the [[p1]]global environment[[p2]]; in addition, each session has a [[p3]]session environment[[p4]]. When a window is created, the session and global environments are merged. If a variable exists in both, the value from the session environment is used. The result is the initial environment passed to the new process.

The [[p0]] session option may be used to update the session environment from the client when a new session is created or an old reattached. [[p1]] also initialises the [[p2]] variable with some internal information to allow commands to be executed from inside, and the [[p3]] variable with the correct terminal setting of ‘[[p4]]’.

Variables in both session and global environments may be marked as hidden. Hidden variables are not passed into the environment of new processes and instead can only be used by tmux itself (for example in formats, see the [[p0]] section).
Commands to alter and view the environment are:

Set or unset an environment variable. If [[p0]] is used, the change is made in the global environment; otherwise, it is applied to the session environment for [[p1]]. If [[p2]] is present, then [[p3]] is expanded as a format. The [[p4]] flag unsets a variable. [[p5]] indicates the variable is to be removed from the environment before starting a new process. [[p6]] marks the variable as hidden.

Display the environment for [[p0]] or the global environment with [[p1]]. If [[p2]] is omitted, all variables are shown. Variables removed from the environment are prefixed with ‘[[p3]]’. If [[p4]] is used, the output is formatted as a set of Bourne shell commands. [[p5]] shows hidden variables (omitted by default).
[[p0]] includes an optional status line which is displayed in the bottom line of each terminal.

By default, the status line is enabled and one line in height (it may be disabled or made multiple lines with the [[p0]] session option) and contains, from left-to-right: the name of the current session in square brackets; the window list; the title of the active pane in double quotes; and the time and date.

Each line of the status line is configured with the [[p0]] option. The default is made of three parts: configurable left and right sections (which may contain dynamic content such as the time or output from a shell command, see the [[p1]], [[p2]], [[p3]], and [[p4]] options below), and a central window list. By default, the window list shows the index, name and (if any) flag of the windows present in the current session in ascending numerical order. It may be customised with the [[p5]] and [[p6]] options. The flag is one of the following symbols appended to the window name:
Window activity is monitored and activity has been detected.
Window bells are monitored and a bell has occurred in the window.
The window has been silent for the [[p0]] interval.
The window contains the marked pane.
The window's active pane is zoomed.
The # symbol relates to the [[p0]] window option. The window name is printed in inverted colours if an alert (bell, activity or silence) is present.
The colour and attributes of the status line may be configured, the entire status line using the [[p0]] session option and individual windows using the [[p1]] window option.
The status line is automatically refreshed at interval if it has changed, the interval may be controlled with the [[p0]] session option.
Commands related to the status line are as follows:
Clear status prompt history for prompt type [[p0]]. If [[p1]] is omitted, then clear history for all types. See [[p2]] for possible values for [[p3]].
Open the command prompt in a client. This may be used from inside [[p0]] to execute commands interactively.
If [[p0]] is specified, it is used as the command. With [[p1]], [[p2]] is expanded as a format.

If [[p0]] is present, [[p1]] is a comma-separated list of the initial text for each prompt. If [[p2]] is given, [[p3]] is a comma-separated list of prompts which are displayed in order; otherwise a single prompt is displayed, constructed from [[p4]] if it is present, or ‘[[p5]]’ if not. [[p6]] disables splitting of [[p7]] and [[p8]] at commas and treats them literally.

Before the command is executed, the first occurrence of the string ‘[[p0]]’ and all occurrences of ‘[[p1]]’ are replaced by the response to the first prompt, all ‘[[p2]]’ are replaced with the response to the second prompt, and so on for further prompts. Up to nine prompt responses may be replaced (‘[[p3]]’ to ‘[[p4]]’). ‘[[p5]]’ is like ‘[[p6]]’ but any quotation marks are escaped.

[[p5]] executes the command every time the prompt input changes instead of when the user exits the command prompt. [[p6]] makes [[p7]] cancel an empty prompt. [[p8]] opens a prompt inside a pane instead of on the status line.
[[p0]] tells [[p1]] the prompt type. This affects what completions are offered when [[p2]] is pressed. Available types are: ‘[[p3]]’, ‘[[p4]]’.

[[p0]] maintains a set of named [[p1]]paste buffers[[p2]]. Each buffer may be either explicitly or automatically named. Explicitly named buffers are named when created with the [[p3]] or [[p4]] commands, or by renaming an automatically named buffer with [[p5]] [[p6]]. Automatically named buffers are given a name such as ‘[[p7]]’, ‘[[p8]]’ and so on. When the [[p9]] option is reached, the oldest automatically named buffer is deleted. Explicitly named buffers are not subject to [[p10]] and may be deleted with the [[p11]] command.

Buffers may be added using [[p0]] or the [[p1]] and [[p2]] commands, and pasted into a window using the [[p3]] command. If a buffer command is used and no buffer is specified, the most recently added automatically named buffer is assumed.
A configurable history buffer is also maintained for each window. By default, up to 2000 lines are kept; this can be altered with the [[p0]] option (see the [[p1]] command above).

Put a pane into buffer mode, where a buffer may be chosen interactively from a list. Each buffer is shown on one line. A shortcut key is shown on the left in brackets allowing for immediate choice, or the list may be navigated and an item chosen or otherwise manipulated using the keys below. [[p0]] zooms the pane. [[p1]] disables any confirmation prompts. The following keys may be used in buffer mode:
Open the buffer in an editor
Enter a format to filter items
After a buffer is chosen, ‘[[p0]]’ is replaced by the buffer name in [[p1]] and the result executed as a command. If [[p2]] is not given, "paste-buffer [[p3]] [[p4]] '[[p5]]'" is used.

[[p0]] specifies the initial sort order: one of ‘[[p1]]’ (time), ‘[[p2]]’, or ‘[[p3]]’. [[p4]] reverses the sort order. [[p5]] specifies an initial filter: the filter is a format - if it evaluates to zero, the item in the list is not shown, otherwise it is shown. If a filter would lead to an empty list, it is ignored. Delete the buffer named [[p0]], or the most recently added automatically named buffer if not specified.
